Read code[-3:] on the cleaned code. The minus sign counts back from the end, so the slice gives '007'. Keeping this result as text preserves the label number.
Keep the original entry separately if support needs to see exactly what Anu typed. The methods produced new text values. They left the original entry available.
strings.outcome: You can clean a search entry, compare it reliably, and preserve identifiers exactly as people see them.
terms: One element of Python text, such as A, 0 or a space; a displayed symbol can contain several such elements.
Text written directly in code between quotation marks.
A position in a string. The first position is 0 and the last can be addressed as -1.
A stretch of text taken from a start position up to an excluded end position.
An operation attached to a value, such as strip() on a piece of text.
A string's characters stay fixed after creation. An edit produces another string.
Placing values into text, for example putting a tracking code inside a delivery message.

decisions.situation: A customer named ' Ana  María ' asks for a tidy greeting but wants the original account entry retained.
decisions.action: Create a display value by joining the words with one space and keep the original entry.
decisions.reason: Splitting on whitespace collects the words; joining them chooses the spacing in the greeting.
decisions.check: The greeting reads 'Hello, Ana María!' and the original account entry still contains the original spaces.
decisions.tradeoff: Some names contain intentional spacing, so the cleaned version serves this greeting only.
decisions.alternative: Overwrite the account name with the cleaned greeting.

decisions.situation: A shelf label 'BX-009' becomes 'BX-9' when the receipt is printed.
decisions.action: Extract the suffix as text and insert those characters into the receipt.
decisions.reason: The suffix identifies a box; treating it as a quantity loses significant zeroes.
decisions.check: A scan of BX-009 matches the printed receipt character for character.
decisions.tradeoff: If the warehouse later needs the numeric sequence, convert a separate copy.
decisions.alternative: Convert the suffix to an integer before composing the receipt.

decisions.situation: An address book needs a case-insensitive search for 'Straße' using the typed word 'STRASSE'.
decisions.action: Build separate comparison keys using casefold() for both names.
decisions.reason: Case folding can map the German sharp s to ss for a caseless comparison.
decisions.check: Both search keys compare equal and the displayed spelling remains Straße.
decisions.tradeoff: Case folding handles case; accent-insensitive or locale-specific matching needs a separate policy.
decisions.alternative: Compare the original address book value with the uppercase search text.

numbers.title: Pack full boxes and count what is left
numbers.story: Dev has 53 mangoes and boxes that hold 6 each. He needs to tell the driver exactly how many sealed boxes and loose mangoes to collect.
steps: Ask how many full groups of 6 fit in 53. Eight groups use 48 mangoes; a ninth group would require 54.
Python writes the full-box calculation as 53 // 6. The answer is 8.
The remainder is 53 % 6, which gives 5. Check the packing slip by combining 8 × 6 + 5 and recovering 53.
numbers.outcome: You can choose the operation that gives a whole-group count, a leftover count or a fractional measurement.
terms: A sign telling the computer which calculation to perform.
The result of division; for full boxes the whole-number quotient counts complete groups.
The part left after making whole groups.
A number stored with a fractional part and limited precision.
The rules deciding which operation happens first when several share a line.

decisions.situation: A bus planner seats 41 people on eight-seat vans and books only five vans.
decisions.action: Count a final extra van when the passenger count has a nonzero remainder.
decisions.reason: Five full vans hold 40 people, leaving one passenger without a seat.
decisions.check: Forty people need five vans and 41 people need six.
decisions.tradeoff: The rounding rule depends on needing space for every passenger.
decisions.alternative: Use the whole-group quotient alone for the vehicle count.

decisions.situation: Three 10-paise charges printed by a billing tool display a tiny unexpected decimal tail.
decisions.action: Keep integer paise for the calculation and format the total as rupees at display time.
decisions.reason: Whole units avoid the binary rounding involved in many decimal fractions.
decisions.check: Ten paise added three times gives 30 paise and displays as ₹0.30.
decisions.tradeoff: Amounts smaller than a paise need an explicit rounding policy.
decisions.alternative: Compare floating-point money totals for exact equality after every addition.

decisions.situation: A worker wants the average of 10 and 20 minutes but types 10 + 20 / 2.
decisions.action: Put the addition in parentheses before dividing by two.
decisions.reason: Division runs before addition unless grouping changes the order.
decisions.check: The revised calculation reports 15 minutes.
decisions.tradeoff: Extra parentheses help readers most when the intended grouping could be ambiguous.
decisions.alternative: Divide only the second time by the number of entries.

conditions.title: Decide who receives the children's ticket
conditions.story: Leela at a museum sells a children's ticket to anyone younger than 12. A predicate is a question about a value with a yes-or-no answer. Here the question is 'Is this visitor's age below 12?' You can answer it before learning any Python.
steps: Take age 11. The comparison 11 < 12 asks whether 11 is smaller than 12. Its answer in Python is True, meaning yes.
Try age 12. The same predicate, age < 12, now gives False. The boundary matters because 'younger than 12' excludes the twelfth birthday.

A different predicate, age == 12, asks whether the two numbers have the same value. At age 12 that answer is True. The double equals sign tests equality; a single equals sign assigns a value to a name.
Use if to choose the children's ticket when age < 12 is True. Use else for the remaining visitors. The comparison answers a question and the branch uses that answer to choose what happens.
conditions.outcome: You can translate an everyday rule into a yes/no test, check its boundary, and explain the decision to a customer.
terms: A test about a value that answers yes or no, such as 'Is the age under 12?'
The computer's two possible truth values, True for yes and False for no.
A question about how values relate, such as smaller than (<) or equal to (==).
A value where a decision changes, such as age 12 in the ticket rule.
One path of instructions selected because a condition has a particular truth value.
A way to require two conditions to both be true for the combined test to pass.

decisions.situation: A shop promises free delivery on orders of ₹500 or more, but an exact ₹500 order is charged.
decisions.action: Test total >= 500 for free delivery.
decisions.reason: The equals part includes the advertised boundary value.
decisions.check: ₹499 attracts a fee, while ₹500 and ₹501 qualify for free delivery.
decisions.tradeoff: The policy must specify whether the comparison uses the total before or after discounts.
decisions.alternative: Use total > 500 and assume customers rarely spend exactly ₹500.

decisions.situation: A cinema grants a student discount only for a valid student card and a weekday screening. A Saturday student currently gets the discount.
decisions.action: Join the valid-card and weekday checks with and.
decisions.reason: The advertised discount requires both facts to hold for the same screening.
decisions.check: A weekday student qualifies; a Saturday student and a weekday nonstudent both pay the regular price.
decisions.tradeoff: A future weekend promotion needs its own explicit rule.
decisions.alternative: Combine the two requirements with or.

decisions.situation: A donation desk gives a gold badge at ₹1,000 and a silver badge at ₹500. A ₹1,200 donor receives silver.
decisions.action: Check the gold threshold first, then test the silver threshold in the next branch.
decisions.reason: A donation above ₹1,000 also passes the ₹500 check, and the first matching branch wins.
decisions.check: ₹1,200 yields gold, ₹700 yields silver and ₹499 receives neither badge.
decisions.tradeoff: Overlapping thresholds need an agreed priority whenever the badge scheme changes.
decisions.alternative: Check the silver threshold first because it is the smaller number.
